utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Mr. Registrar, have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the interpreters hear me? Very well. Can Defence counsel hear? Can Prosecution counsel hear? The accused, Mr. Jelisic, would you please rise and tell us how you feel? THE ACCUSED JELISIC: [Interpretation] My health condition has not really improved, but we decided not to disrupt the court proceedings, and out of respect for you, Your Honours, and the witnesses who suffered a lot in Brcko and have travelled all the way over here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If you have any problems at all -- please be seated. If you have any problems, do not hesitate to ask for the floor, and we'll find a solution. I was asked, and I agreed, that there be a nurse nearby, if necessary. I think that we can now resume our trial and perhaps ask the Prosecutor to bring in the next witness. I think this is a public hearing, at least that's what the registrar told me, that we would be in public hearing. Is that correct? Yes, that is. Mr. Nice, would you tell us who the next witness is? I believe he had already come in and already taken an oath. That is Witness G.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed it is, and because it's a protected witness, the screens must come down, but only briefly while he comes in. I'm happy to tell Your Honour that the five witnesses whose summaries were provided yesterday are not the subject of any contest so far as the Defence is concerned. They are content for them to be called. They won't take very long, as you'll see from the summaries, and I'll make arrangements for their travel accordingly. I'm further happy to tell Your Honour that Mr. Greaves has been extremely helpful this morning in agreeing that certain parts of the statement summary of Witness G may indeed be simply presented to him in a led form, and I'm grateful to him for that, and that will save some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We agree to that in order to save as much time as possible, thanks to you, but we are imposing nothing on the Defence. The Defence will conduct the cross-examination as it sees fit. I encourage the Defence to try to save as much time as possible, but I can only encourage him to do so. However, I am asking you, insofar as possible, Mr. Prosecutor, if you consider it desirable, to use your summaries which were given to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, we have a question that we're concerned with. We would like to ask it before the witness comes in. As regards the summary of Witness G's statement, are you going to ask for it as an admission as an exhibit or are you not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It had not originally been my intention to ask for them to be exhibited. They were, as I think I characterised them, a tool to help the Tribunal know what evidence could be given and so on. Yesterday, Your Honour decided that an appropriate way forward would be for the witness to acknowledge the summary as effectively a document of his and to sign it and for it then to be produced. That could only be done if the witness, being literate, had read a version himself in a language he understands, alternatively has had read to him by an interpreter a version in a language he does not understand. With this witness, I understand that he has this morning gone through the B/C/S version and is, indeed, in a position, if this is what the Court would find appropriate, is in a position to sign it, and it can then become an exhibit. With a later witness, who is either not literate or less literate, he would only be able to acknowledge a version as having been something he believes to have been read over to him by an interpreter. But on that basis, he could sign it as well. So I'm quite happy to do that, but notwithstanding the witness's signing of it, I shall be taking him through some of the important parts that I understand to be in dispute with the Defence. But I shall, of course, be able to do things so much more quickly with the aid of this tool. I hope that's acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have any problems with that, Mr. Greaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, strictly speaking, a summary is not evidence. But if the witness acknowledges it, then of course that becomes part of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We can have Witness G brought into the courtroom now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you hear me, Witness G?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please be seated, Witness G. I believe you have already taken the oath. You can now be seated. Thank you for being patient.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure all of the problems that occurred yesterday have been explained to you which were the cause of the postponement of your testimony, but I think that now there are no further problems. Mr. Prosecutor must have spoken to you about the summary of the various statements you made. It will be very important for you to indicate whether you recognise this or acknowledge this summary as being valid as expressing your statements, because if necessary, we're going to use it as an exhibit. But we will let the Prosecutor do his work. Mr. Nice, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you look at this piece of paper that's being shown --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone to the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My apologies. Will you look, please, at this piece of paper that's being shown to you, and say nothing except "Yes" or "No" in answer to the question. Is that your name?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the usher would be so good as to just show this document to the witness, please. Just hand it to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness G, is this a document that was shown to you last night and that you were able to read?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it accurate?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could you please just put your name -- you will be given a pen; perhaps you could just put your name at the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the problem is it's Witness G for this Court. I think, if he produces the document and acknowledges its accuracy on our transcript, that makes the connection between the document, its accuracy, and the witness, and avoids any name having to be given which would then have to be withdrawn or withheld. Copies available for the Court in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Mr. Nice. You said exactly what I was going to say. The connection between the witness and his own acknowledgement of the document must be indicated, and once that's indicated in the transcript, I think that will be enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Court already has copies of this document in English and French, and I'll be grateful at some stage for the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Prosecution Exhibit 15, 15A for the French version and 15B for the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness G, I'm going to ask you to deal with the following question simply by telling me if what I propose is correct. Resident in Brcko when the bridges were blown on the 30th of April of 1992, did your family stay with relations in Moaca while you stayed at your home in Kolobara, a Muslim area, where you helped to organise patrols to protect homes; over the next few days, was there an escalation in military activity with trucks carrying military personnel seen arriving in Brcko sporting artillery and could -- I beg your pardon -- with artillery and small-arms fire being heard coming from neighbouring hamlets? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 4th of May, were you, with others, hiding in the basement of a neighbour's house when you were expelled by Serb military forces and marched to the town mosque; on departure from the area of your house, did you see that it, along with other houses, was on fire?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you detained at the mosque for two days, while there, women and children were being separated from men of military age, and they were taken away in vehicles?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While at the mosque, paragraph 5, was there a man called or known as Papa who you saw dealt with in a particular way? And it's not necessary -- you can look at the -- with the Court's leave, you can look at the summary, but I would be quite happy if you can deal with this from your own memory, unless you have any difficulty. Was there a man known as Papa, and what happened to him? In just a sentence.

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, there was. He was taken out into the hallway. He was beaten, and later he was taken across over there to the hospital, and then he was led away. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 6th of May, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 6th of May, we were transferred from the mosque, in trucks, to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When there, was there a person you got to know and recognise wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: While we were standing in front of the building where we were kept, I noticed a person in a blue uniform with a bandaged hand talking to a group of prisoners. I approached in order to hear what was being said, and then I heard this man say, "70 per cent of you should be killed, 30 per cent should be dealt with and beaten up," and then, out of those numbers, maybe about 3 per cent were all right. And then he said, "All of you are going to come to me," and cursed our balija mothers. I did not know this person at the time. Only when I arrived in Luka did I recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did you arrive in Luka?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I arrived in Luka on the 8th of May, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you arrived there, where did you first wait?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: We waited by the first hangar, to the left of the hangar and facing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can the witness look at this document, please, which, although it's similar to an earlier exhibit, it may perhaps serve a useful purpose. It's a little clearer, I think, and will, I think, become Exhibit 16.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Prosecution Exhibit 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness G, if you wish to point something out on the photograph, the usher will hand you a pointer. Stay in your seat, in order to preserve your facial anonymity, and use the pointer in your hand to indicate things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think that you're straining the machine a little; we've lost our picture. Thank you very much. There's a mistake there, I think, in the -- thank you. Something's seriously wrong. Can the video be turned off, please? I don't know what's gone wrong, Your Honour, if Your Honour is looking at the video.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There's a technical problem. The video booth has just told me there's a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, the wrong image entirely is coming up on the screen. Yes, can you press "Video Evidence"? I'm sure the Chamber has. You see the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the public gallery, what's happening?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to have the public taken out of the public gallery, unless the problem has been solved, because we saw the hangar on the video, we saw the photograph. Can that be checked?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While the technical matter is being addressed, of course, I can take or the Tribunal can take appropriate steps in relation to the delayed video. That's not a problem. As to the incorrect transmission of current images, it may be that the Chamber would -- would Your Honour just give me one minute? I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The registrar can assure you, Witness G, that your image was not projected into the public gallery. Perhaps we should have all of the face image distorted. Do you understand what I've just said? You can be assured that we're not going to have to take any other special measures in respect of what was on the monitor, because the public gallery didn't see it. Perhaps we could then raise the blinds so this be a public session, but be sure that we do not show the witness's face. After this problem, the witness may wonder whether he's not being pursued by bad luck.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There is a problem which is continuing. We cannot have the camera on Witness G. There's a problem with his face. We can continue to question the witness, but the camera will focus only on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does everybody agree, my colleagues agree, agree that we proceed that way? Very well. Mr. Nice, after having reassured our witness, we can now continue the hearing in public session, since his image is completely distorted. All right, Mr. Nice, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Looking at this exhibit and using the pointer, can you show us where it was you first waited on arrival at the Luka camp?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not know whether I shall be able to show you exactly where I stood on that occasion on this photograph, because I don't see the end of these hangars. We were standing to the left from the first hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May he see Exhibit 10 instead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you point on this photograph to where it was that you first stood and waited?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes [indicating].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many people, approximately, were waiting there at the time of your arrival?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were seven of us in a group. Across from us, if I may put it that way, that is, on the other side of the entrance, there were about 30 people or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While waiting there, did you see the man who had spoken to you at the barracks, the man in the blue uniform?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where was he when you first saw him? What was he doing?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: When I saw him first, he was standing by that room into which detainees were being taken. So when I saw him first, he was entering that room. After that, he took out a detainee and quietly took him to the right or, rather, towards the corner of the building, further away from the door. He was followed by another individual in a uniform and armed too, and they turned the corner of the building. From there, I heard shots, and after that, that individual in a blue uniform, and subsequently when he comes close to us, I will see him properly and learn that his name is Goran. Then he went back into the room that he had come out. After that, he took out another witness and took him --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can the witness have Exhibit 16 back on the ELMO, the other photograph. Thank you. That is a closer view of the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we see in this photograph, although the photograph was taken years later, can we see in this photograph the doorway to which and from which the man in the blue uniform went?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, even though this office seems to be demolished by now, but this corner that I meant was here [indicating], it is this part, and the door is up there [indicating]. There, here, [indicating] the door leading into those offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So let us return to your account of the second person you saw leaving that office with the man you discovered was called Goran. What did the man Goran do?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was taking this prisoner in front of him, and he also took him around the corner, behind the corner of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: After they disappeared around the corner, what happened? What, if anything, did you hear?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Shots were heard from that direction, and after that, Goran returned alone to the same building that he had come out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see a third detainee leave that office?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: The third detainee was pushed out of that office. I believe his face was covered with blood. He turned to Goran, and he merely indicated to him the direction in which he should go in front of him, and they started towards the corner of the building. But even as the detainee reached that corner, Goran fired at the back of his head, and I saw the detainee fall. After that, Goran approached the group that I was with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you say the man fell, did he fall, so far as you could judge, dead, or was he still alive, or what was the position?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was dead. He was -- he partly fell down behind that corner, but we could still see his legs on this side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The man Goran approached your group. What, if anything, did he say or do?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: When he approached our group, he told us to empty our pockets, all that we had there, our money, valuables, documents, and we put it all here at the corner of this hangar. There was an old car, unusable car, and we put it on the hood of that car. He collected all of this, and he said that this was all intended for the families of fallen Serb combatants. As he took it away, he told us sardonically that he could guarantee that we would not live to see the morning there. So he took these things away, and came back again, and took us into the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the hangar, did you see the man Goran again shortly thereafter or at any time thereafter?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did see him shortly thereafter. He entered the hangar, was asking for three volunteers. He did not wait for them to apply. He pointed, "You, you, and you," and the person sitting next to me stood up and went out, that is, he took them out. They went out. After a while, that person came back. I could see that he was all shook up, that he was very emotional, so I asked him, "What happened?" He told me that he had to carry -- he said, "I carried a man and threw him onto a pile, and yet I can feel his heart beat." He was very shaken by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That night, what happened so far as detainees in the hangar were concerned? Did they all stay there or did any of them leave? If so, what were the circumstances of their leaving?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: During that night, the detainees were taken out in foursomes. I would be alerted every time they would come in, open the door and put the lights on, but then they took three men next to me out and they didn't come back. I really had it very hard, and I remember one case when people were taken out, after which Goran returned very quickly, because on that particular occasion one of the detainees said, "In a year, the machine gun will fire again." Then he was back in no time at all and said, "Which one of you said that the machine gun would bark again within a year?" That man said, "I did," and so he went out too. I know he returned after about half an hour or so. We did not expect him to come back alive. But I noted that somebody sitting next to him asked him, "So how was it?" He turned to him and blew in his face or something like that, and he seemed to be reeking of alcohol. So they were taking people out until late into the night. I can't really say because I lost my sense of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you say they took them out in foursomes, at what interval of time did they go out in foursomes? If you can put an interval on it.

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it was about half an hour. Something like that. I'm not really sure; about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did any, some, or all of the foursomes come back? What happened?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not see them come back, but I must also confess that at that particular time, I wasn't paying much attention because I was really concerned about my own fate, and I was trying to tell myself to persuade myself that I would survive regardless of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see anything else of the man, Goran, in the hangar that night?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did. It was after midnight. He entered the hangar and said he would not kill any more if we knew how to sing a Serb song, "Who Says Who Lies," and if we could sing it three times without making a mistake. And after that, we all sang, and he was very happy, and he sort of conducted our singing. And after that, he called all of those would were outside to enter and see the balija singing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The following day, the 9th of May, you started the day in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see something of a man called Stipo Glavocevic?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us very briefly what happened to him, and if you can, at what time of the day.

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was in the morning. Goran brought him to the hangar, and I know he was quite merry, so he put him in the middle of the hangar and told us, "Here's your Stipo walking around the town." And after that, he put on a serious mien and said, "Well, he has killed three Serbs; which one of you will kill him?" And he started offering his gun to each one of us, but none of the detainees would take it. And as he reached the end, here, on the right-hand side, I know that at that moment, Stipo asked us, "Come on, fellows, why doesn't one of you kill me?" And Goran heard it, so he came back to our side and started again offering the gun to us, but none of us would take it. And there was another guard in a uniform, I believe the reserve uniform, that is, the uniform of the reserve forces, and he said, "Let me kill him; I haven't killed an Ustasha since July." And Goran told Stipo to get out immediately. And I know there was yet another guard who had a long sword or a sabre, and he hit Stipo on the back with the blunt side of that weapon, and they took him out and to the left, and they went in the other direction. And then I heard a shot and the passage of the refrigerating truck. But from the place where I was, I could not see that murder. However, from other inmates to the right and left of me, I heard that he had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just two supplementary questions. What ethnicity was Stipo? Did you know what he did before this conflict, and what condition was he in when he was brought in by Goran?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Stipo was a Croat by origin. I believe that his last job was with Bimeks; I do not know if he was retired. And what condition he was in, well, he arrived in a suit, but he was all bloody, and there was a puddle of blood under his feet where he had stood in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A man, a detainee called Jasce, can you tell us about that man?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. As regards Jasce, I remember Goran entered the hangar and said, "Who's the one who cursed a Serb woman's mother? I'll take him out." And he was taken out, and I did not see him again. And I really do not have anything else to say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A woman called Naza Bukvic --

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- what can you tell us about her? Time of day, again, if you can help.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As regards Naza Bukvic, the time of the event is the 9th of May. It was then when I was issued a pass that I could leave the camp, and so I came out of this office which I mentioned before to which we went and where we were interrogated, and, at that moment, I could not get through because on my way I saw Goran beat Naza. She was sitting on the grass, and he had one baton in every hand, in every hand he had a baton, and I couldn't pass by because he was there, simply, he was on my way. And he looked towards me, he spread his arms, and he said, "Her brother is a sniper," and went on beating her. She was all covered in blood. Her clothes were torn. And he went on beating her, and I managed to pass by them. And then, after that, I stopped for a while, and I was there for another five minutes or so hoping that through that person who had helped me get out, perhaps help also my uncle who had stayed behind in a hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just point on the photograph, if you can, with the pointer, whereabouts it was that Goran was beating the woman.

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot show it in this photograph because it was a bit further down. I came out of this room and started down that way, and so it was further down there [indicating].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If he could just briefly have the other photograph in front of him, please, photograph number 10, exhibit number 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does that show the place?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Here, in the grass [indicating].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you were --

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Here, in this area, on the grass, here [indicating].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. You've spoken of your interrogation; I needn't trouble you with that, either at all or barely at all. Were you interrogated once, or more than once?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Later? I'm sorry, I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you interrogated, yourself, once or more than once?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean there, in Luka?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, in Luka.

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Once.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it by Goran or by someone else?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. You explained that you managed to get a pass to get out. In a sentence, who was it who enabled you to get out of this particular place?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would prefer not to mention the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: But he was wearing a uniform of the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was he somebody you had known from before?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as a result of that, paragraph 22, were you released from Luka; did you move elsewhere for some couple of months, until July; you thereafter went to the Batkovic detention centre and were exchanged in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The man, Goran, you saw him at the barracks and here at Luka; did you ever see him again?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I saw him on another two occasions, but I did not have any contact with him. The first time was in Batkovic. He was on the other side of the fence; some prisoners approached the fence. I did not want to do that. And the next time was when I was exchanged at Grbavica, because everybody in the bus was pointing at Goran, because they were afraid of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you at any stage get to know a name other than Goran for this man?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the camp, Goran was the only name I heard of. Later I learned that his last name was Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From whom did you learn that, or how did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe it was from those who were there with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure whether in light of the fact that paragraphs 19, 20, and 21 reflect counts in the indictment that have already been responded to in a particular way, I'm not sure whether identity will be an issue, but I propose to ask this next question of the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Witness G, please just confine your answer to this question to just "Yes" or "No"; do you understand me? I'm going to ask you a question, and I want you just to say to it "Yes" or "No." Would you feel able, now, to identify the person, Goran, if you saw him again? And please, just answer that question "Yes" or "No."

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I propose to ask the obvious question, in the absence of restraint.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you see him here today?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Point him out, please.

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: [Witness complies] I am certain that this is this creature whom I have called Goran Jelisic in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The witness identified the defendant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Witness G. You will be asked further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me thank you, Mr. Nice, for using the summary in a way that I think is completely consistent, which was the very purpose of our work, that is, to allow the oral and written facts to be expressed by the witness. And now we can have the cross-examination, but I would simply like to ask Mr. Greaves how much time he needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I was going to ask my learned friend that he indicated that he was going to ask about the names on the list, and he may well have forgotten to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to Mr. Greaves. I had omitted to deal with that. And if the witness could have, please, the two lists. First the -- which exhibit number is it? First the longer list, which is -- I can't remember the number of the exhibit -- 12. It's 12. Yes, we can always use the same exhibit, Exhibit 12, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been asked before to look at this list of names and to go through them to see if you can recognise any of the names, either as people you knew or people of whose fate you were aware, or, indeed, if there were any people that you had seen since your being held at Luka. On page 1, and in the middle of the page, a little bit over halfway down, there's a name, Cembic. Was that a name that you knew of?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did you know of him?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I knew this person from before the war. He was at my house on the 1st of May, 1992, and then went with the meat that he had bought, went home, and later I heard that he had been labelled as a sniper and was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Four names up from the bottom, Glavocevic, Stipo? Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, this is the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already described his fate in my statement. It is Glavocevic, Stipo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Hadzic, Suad, second from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I knew Suad Hadzic. I met him at the barracks. He had left on an earlier bus, I don't know where, but I did not see him after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Second sheet, two thirds of the way down, Kartal, Kasim. Did you know that name?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I knew him even before the war. I did not see them during or after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Third sheet, a third of the way down, Muranjkovic, Galib. Known to you?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: From before the war; I did not see him during or after the war. But as far as I know, when I was in Batkovic, his son was brought there, and that he had been taken off that vehicle on the way there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Fourth sheet, two thirds of the way down, Terzic, T-E-R-Z-I-C, Mohamed?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I knew Mohamed personally. I was friends with him, and I knew his brothers from sight. We were together in the mosque, and I saw them in Luka in a group of 30 who were released before the curfew, and I heard that they were killed at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you seen any of the people on that list, to your knowledge, since the events that you have described?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. You mean the ones we mentioned now? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next list, please. Would Your Honours just give me a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On sheet 1 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: He's turned his microphone off, and I don't think he'll be heard by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On sheet 1, the second name, is that the Papa that you've already spoken of?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The same sheet, number 11, Irfan Topalcevic?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Topalcevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, Topalcevic with an "a". What was know to you of him?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happened to him, according to your understanding?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I knew him personally before the war. I did not see him during or after the war. I heard that he was killed at home at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Number 15 at the bottom of the sheet, Muhamed Jakubovic, also known as Ulika?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him. I know that he was killed in the period after I was released from Luka and when I was held in my neighbourhood. My information is that he was making equipment for -- harnesses for horses and that he was killed by one of the guys who worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next sheet, number 16, Sakib Becirevic?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I knew him before the war. I did not see him during or after the war. I heard that he was killed behind the gymnasium and that Ranko Cesic was the one who killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Number 17, Dr. Edhemovic?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I only knew him before the war. I did not see him during or after.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you hear of his fate?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I heard that he was killed, only that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 19, 20, and 21, the brothers Terzic, you've spoken of one already. What did you hear of these three?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: They returned from Luka and went to Kolobara, where they lived. My information is that Kosta, the Chetnik, killed them, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 23, Sulejmanovic?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him before the war. I met him during the war when I was exchanged. I think it was on the 4th or 5th of October 1992. While I was in the bus, he was walking around in town, wearing a suit. I don't know his subsequent fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you saw him in October 1992, and you don't know what's happened about him since then. Number 36 on the next sheet, Osman Vatic?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I did not know him before the war, and I met him in Batkovic. I know that he was released home from Batkovic, and I also heard that he was killed as soon as he returned home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to take a short break. The afternoon is long. I suggest that we take a 15-minute break and start again at 3.30 or 3.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, and please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we resume and before I give the floor to Mr. Greaves, my colleagues and myself would like to speak to your interpreter, Mr. Londrovic and Mr. Greaves. Your interpreter, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I haven't introduced her, and I regret the discourtesy of not doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We're going to ask her to stand, because we would -- please stand. We, of course, agree that you be here. I wanted to know what -- I asked Mrs. de Sampayo what your status was, and that is all correct. But nonetheless, I simply wanted not to have you take an oath, that would take place at another place, but to call your attention to the confidentiality which must reign throughout these proceedings. We simply wish to say this to you in a more official, solemn manner. I should have done it as soon as we started working yesterday, but I wanted to take advantage of this time in order to make you fully mindful of those responsibilities. All right?

utterances.speaker: MS. ZIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I more or less understood. You may be seated. I understood what you said, and I thank you very much. All right, Mr. Greaves, the floor is yours. You are going to conduct the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. Could I just say about my interpreter, she's been working for me and for other counsel for over two years. She worked with us in the Celebici trial. She has also, for a period, worked on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor. She has the confidence of everybody that I've ever met that she is entirely aware of all the requirements of confidentiality. I hope that's also a further assurance to Your Honour. She's further aware of what is required of her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine. You yourself, I assume, are mindful of your own obligations. Can you tell us how long your cross-examination is going to last? I'm sure that you've got a mind which has been synthesised just as brilliantly as your adversary or your opponent on the other side of the bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour is too kind. Your Honour, I hope to be about an hour and a half. Can I give you the usual caveat that all lawyers, I'm afraid, give, which is that sometimes things develop, which means you go on longer, or sometimes my estimations are totally wrong and one runs over a bit. But I'm aiming at about an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that you understand fully the totality of these proceedings, let me remind you that the examination in chief, thanks to the new method which the Prosecutor is using, and even if you don't completely agree with that method, the examination in chief lasted for 45 minutes. I've noted what you have just said, but I ask that you not repeat yourself. Please do not have the witness repeat things that he may have already said. All right. Let's begin, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Witness G, I'm going to ask you some questions now, please. Could you remember, please, this, that whilst I ask you the questions, if there is a question which you do not understand, please do not be shy. Stop me, if you do not understand it, and ask me immediately that I repeat it or rephrase it. Is that acceptable to you?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. G, I would like to ask you this, please, to start off with: When you made a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, you described yourself as, at that time, being a soldier in the BiH army. Is that an occupation or an engagement that you continue to have? Are you still in the BiH army or have you left it?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You've left?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, no, I'm with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You're still in the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I ask you this? I don't want to ask the details, for you to identify any particular unit or regiment, but are you connected in any way with military intelligence, in your occupation as a BiH soldier, or the intelligence services in any way?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't want to know any more than that. Mr. G, prior to the outbreak of conflict in Brcko, were you in any way active in political life in the town?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: During the conflict, did you take part in politics? Did you become a party member of any kind?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Have you become a member of, for example, the SDA since the conflict?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I am not a member of any political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Very well. I suspect that you've been staying in The Hague for a couple of days, at the very least, and you've been through the statements which you made firstly to the BiH authorities, the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities, and to the OTP, and so you're familiar with those two documents?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Apart from those two statements, Mr. G, have you made a statement of any kind to any other authority concerning these matters?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want to turn now, please, to the period immediately before the commencement of conflict in Brcko. I think at the end of April 1992, and I don't want to ask the details of this, but you were concerned about your family -- someone in your family's medical condition, as a result of which you had to go out and be in the town?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: As a result of that, you found yourself in the area of, presumably, the central area --

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm sorry. As a result of having to go out, you found yourself in the centre of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not leave. It was my family which left. I'm afraid I didn't understand your previous question. I was at home throughout, and that is where I was captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I understand that. I'm asking about the last part of April 1992, before your family left, and in particular about the 30th of April. Did you go into the town that day?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It was during that trip that you heard the explosions or explosions were heard; is that right?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I heard an explosion, and after the explosion is when I went into town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Right. Then were you aware of checkpoints having been set up in the town?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, on the outskirts of the town. I knew there were checkpoints set up around the town, but at that moment there were no checkpoints within the town limits.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The checkpoints on the town periphery, were those checkpoints only of one group of people, or were some of them Serbian checkpoints, some of them Muslim checkpoints; can you help us about that?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: The checkpoints that I know about were manned by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Now, after hearing the explosions and going into town, you eventually, I think, came towards the bridge.

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is this right? There had been a number of casualties as a result of whatever had happened at the bridge?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Help us with your recollection, please. Are we talking about two or three casualties, or tens of casualties, or hundreds of casualties?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot really estimate the number of casualties. I did not go into town so as to see that. I went out to find the pacifier for the child, because it had broken, so that the mother could feed him. Then I saw a group of men, and I saw those uniformed men who would not allow anyone to get to the bridge. What I could see were things scattered all over. I saw how people were being turned in various directions to see whether it was an arm or a leg. Somebody said that it was behind the municipal hall, a head or something. Then I went down practically to the mouth of the Brka River into the Sava. There was also a group which was looking at things scattered around and parts of bodies on the grass there, and it was quite crowded. We really had to find an appropriate place to see what was going on. But I realised what had happened, and I really didn't feel like counting. That is all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I didn't want you to think that I was suggesting to you that you should have stayed there to count. I was just trying to get an idea of how many people had been involved and either killed or wounded as a result of this explosion. Would it be fair to say that it probably wasn't as many as 100 but it was more than ten or something like that? Would that be fair? If I'm not right about that, please say so.

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That's a fair comment?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that that would be, yes, the correct estimate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You've been most helpful. It was as a result of, no doubt, that that you got your family away from Brcko. Did you then have conversations with members of your family?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And I don't want to know about where your family went to or anything like that. Does it come to this, that you then sought, you and your family -- male members of your family sought to get information about what was going on and what you should do?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And were some representatives sent to the local community office to find out what was going on, and a particular individual went to check?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they were sent, but I had already prevailed upon my family to leave home, which means that I was at home when those representatives were sent to the neighbourhood community.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I just clarify this. By 1992, I think you were aged 34; is that right? 33 or 34? Born in 1958?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I guess so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Had you, prior to 1992, done your JNA military service, compulsory service?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was one of the things that you were interested in at that stage -- and I don't criticise in any way you for doing this -- but were you interested in what steps you should take towards helping to protect your neighbourhood? Was that one of the reasons why you sent representatives to the local community?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't go there, to our neighbourhood community. It was another person, and we sent him to go there and see what was going on, because we could see what was in the offing, and we wanted to see whether there would be any resistance or whether it would be just left to take its course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In light of the information that you were given, did you and others then organise a number of patrols, armed patrols?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: We organised guards in our street, and that was all. There was nothing else there to be organised. We avoided any contact with any person we did not know. We did not communicate with neighbouring streets either.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you observe -- well, sorry, let me just ask this. Did you have at least one weapon, one firearm with you? Or was it more?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: One. We had one hunting rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So that we have an accurate idea of where this is all taking place, what area of Brcko were you based in?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Next to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you, during the course of the guard duties that you undertook, did you come across, see anything of other patrols that had been formed?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: We noticed to the left and to the right some groups, but were they patrols or something else, I don't know. We avoided any contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would those groups, would you have seen those in the Kolobara and Maoca areas?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Just, again, so that we get the detail. Kolobara, is that an area which was, at that time, of mixed ethnicity but with a Muslim majority?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And by "mixed," I mean Muslim, Serb, and indeed, Croat.

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you help us about Maoca? Can you just describe the ethnic makeup of that district? I'm sorry, I've been told on my left that I'm not pronouncing it correctly, but I hope you understand the area I'm talking about, Mr. G.

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Maoca, yes. The structure was more or less the same as in Kolobara. The Muslims were a majority there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to turn now to May the 1st, and would it be fair to say that's the first day of any degree of fighting taking place between the two communities?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And the first that you were able to see of it were soldiers, in a vehicle, wearing a black hat with a cockade on? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: From your experience in the army and so on, would you be able to say or identify who those troops were and which side they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as this statement about the troops is concerned, this was a column which was moving and which had -- there was this person with a fur hat and a cockade, and these were the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And in due course, you became aware that shooting had started; I think the phrase that you have used is "shooting." Is that small-arms fire, or small arms and artillery, or what?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: It started out with small-arms fire on the other side of town on the 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: "It started out with ..." Did artillery join in later on the 1st of May, or was it exclusively small arms?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Later, later, you could hear explosions too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And are you able to determine whether that was artillery, in the sense of field guns, or was that mortar fire?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what period. Which date in May?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: May the 1st.

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: On May the 1st, as I said, it started out with small-arms fire and maybe an occasional explosion. This is how it started out, and that is what went on into the night. I cannot say exactly, for these explosions, when they occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And could you identify the area of Brcko in which that was taking place?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was in the area of town opposite from the part of town where I was. It was the Dizdarusa section.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And then did there follow about two days when it was relatively quiet? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And did you hear, on May the 3rd, from an acquaintance, something to the effect that the soldiers were not coming further into the town but that most of the town except for Kolobara had been taken over?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Again, on the --

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: That they would not cross Brka, over here, but the centre of town and that area, they were already there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And again, on May the 3rd, was there some degree of small-arms fire that you could hear during the course of the day?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 3rd of May, the artillery fire started, and the explosions, immediately followed by small-arms fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Firstly, could you determine from where the artillery was coming, and could you determine where it was landing?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: The shells were flying over my head, and they were falling in the section of Meraja, Vici, and in the area of Suljaga Sokak, in those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And the area you've described, is that a residential area, the area that the shelling was landing?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Muslim population, with Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And would you describe the shelling that day as intense or sporadic? What would be the right answer?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Intense.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think that as a result of that you decided that you were going to be safest in your basement, and --

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: -- did you become aware that small-arms fire was also taking place, but in two directions, rather than just the one of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And can you help me about this, Mr. G? Either at the time or subsequently, have you learnt whether people were killed as a result of the military activity that was taking place at that time? Or, indeed, did you witness any bodies lying in the street, or anything like that, that were obviously victims of fighting?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I was in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you hear subsequently of people being killed, or when you came out, did you see that?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not see it when I came out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The shelling and shooting, did that stop at nightfall or did it continue during the hours of darkness?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Throughout the night, there was both shelling and there was shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think that the next day, the 4th of May, you heard some shooting, but it subsequently became quiet, leading you to believe the fighting might have been over?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And I think -- and I don't want to go into the detail of it in any way, but there was an incident with a soldier about to throw a hand grenade, which -- that incident was prevented?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And from their uniforms you concluded that they were the Serb volunteer guards; is that right?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And would another name for them be the Arkan soldiers?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You weren't able to leave, I think, at that stage, but were allowed to go back in the basement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was there any further fighting on the 4th of May?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 4th of May, I was at the mosque. Shooting could be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You were subsequently that day moved to the mosque. On your way, did you see military forces in the street or near the hospital yard?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I saw soldiers along the entire length of the street and between the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And were they the same ones that you had seen earlier, the Serb volunteer guards, or were they regular troops, or what kind of troops were they?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Those were the ones who found us in the basement, the Serb volunteer guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. G, I would like to ask you now, please, about the mosque. When you got there, were there already people detained there or were you the first ones?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was not among the first. There were already people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many people were there?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Again, it's a question of my estimate. It was a little less than half of the entire space in which we were kept, and now, I don't know how to estimate that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to do your best. I don't want an exact figure, Mr. G; I know it's difficult. Is it a large mosque, small mosque? What's the sort of size of the mosque you would -- can you give us an idea of that?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was a regular mosque. It was this one larger space, and there was a smaller one, and we were put in this bigger one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If I can just explore it a little further. After you arrived, were other people brought in after you arrived?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, other people were brought in after my arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You've described the -- as best you can at the moment -- the size, but again, if we can use this method, are we talking about just 30 or 40 people, or 100-plus people, or 1.000 people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think you've already asked the question. Please move to another question. I think that you've already asked it, and he has answered as best he can. Please move along.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I didn't pursue the question earlier on because I was thinking how best to put it to him, but I hadn't completed it. Please, can I just try and help him to help you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. Please move to another question. Move to another question. We've spoken a great deal about the mosque already. You've asked him to describe whether it's big, small, average. The witness has answered as best he can. Please move to another question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I would like you to help us, please, Mr. G, about who was in control at the mosque. Were they soldiers, were they police? What sort of people were in control at the mosque?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the mosque, we were guarded by soldiers of the Serb volunteer guard. And different, other military groups could enter the mosque wearing different types of insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is this right that, at that stage, women were separated from you?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: As well as women being separated, were any people who were under 18 taken away, or people who were obviously elderly and unfit for military service?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that inside there were also those younger than 18, and also elderly. It was only later that they were taken away from the mosque, not right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So to clarify, the women were taken away first but at a later stage, on a later day, young people and elderly people were taken away?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you now about an incident which took place on the first night, Mr. G, involving, I think, a man called Enes Turkusic. Do you recall that name?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Turkusic; yes, I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You knew him, and what, knew him from before the war?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And is this right, that he managed to escape from the building, from the mosque building?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you hear anything either immediately after these events or in subsequent years as to what had happened to him after his escape?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I heard it later. I heard that he was killed on the 24th or 25th of May, that he had attempted to swim across the Sava River and was pulled out at Kolobara.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And was that information given to you from a source that you trusted and thought was reliable?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to turn now, please, to the man who was killed on that occasion. I think you knew of him as Kike; is that right?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Kike.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you know that person from before the war?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you learn at the time what his full name was, or have you learnt it subsequently?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I offer a name to you and see whether it rings any bells: Kike Suljic?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but I did not know that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I just clarify. You confirm that that may well have been the name, but you didn't know it at the time?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. G, that's helpful. Did you become aware that person's brother was also being held at the mosque?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is this right, that at some stage, I think probably during the first night, somebody called Kosta came to the mosque?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he came around frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And was he someone that you knew from before the war, or was this the first time that you had come across him?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I saw him then for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And can you describe the man that you called Kosta, can you give a description of him? Age, build, colour of hair, height, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: He had a dark complexion, looked like a Gypsy, as people say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Apart from that, can you say how old he was?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Again, it's a matter of judgement. Perhaps my age.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was he bigger than you, smaller than you?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: He wasn't as tall as I was. He was shorter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Just for the record, how tall are you, Mr. G?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I would like you to look at --

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know if you want a drawing of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: No, thank you. You're being very helpful, and your answers are most concise, if I may say so. Thank you very much, Mr. G. I would like you to look at a photocopy of a photograph, please, the Defence exhibit shown to the other witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Try to remain as close as you can to the examination in chief. Let me remind you of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you please look at the photograph, Mr. G? That photograph may well be quite an old photograph dating from the mid or early 1980s. Is that the man that you knew as Kosta? Can you say? If you can't, just say so.

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: He's very light-skinned here. I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: All right, thank you. I would like now to turn, please, to May the 6th, Mr. G. That's the date on which I think you were transferred to the barracks. Can you say --

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: -- how many people were transferred to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was on a truck that was fully loaded. We were packed, and we almost couldn't fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was there only one truck in use or was there other trucks used to transport you that day?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe it wasn't just one, but I cannot recall at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. G, you have said that at the barracks, you saw Goran and Kosta?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You say that on the 6th of May, he was wearing -- the man Goran was wearing a bandage?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not say that it was on the 6th of May. It was when he was at the barracks, but I cannot say what date that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: How many days were you at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I arrived on the 6th, and I was transferred to Luka on the 8th, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: What you told the Office of the Prosecutor was that you were transferred by bus to the army barracks on the 6th, and you then described how you were taken to the front room of the building by soldiers, and that you saw Goran on that occasion and you [sic] had a bandage on his wrist. Does that refresh your memory as to the date when you saw him with a bandage?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as that statement is concerned, that we were transferred to the barracks from the mosque, I don't know about that statement. From what document is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It's the statement which you made to the Office of the Prosecutor on two dates in February and March 1995, Mr. G, so not the statement that you made to the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities.

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that I was on a truck. I don't know about this other thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You see, what I suggest is that if, as you assert, that was Goran Jelisic, Goran Jelisic had not at that time, the 6th of May, been injured in such a way that he had to wear a bandage and that you are either mistaken or being untruthful about him being at the barracks that day.

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: On which day, on which day?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The 6th of May, Mr. G.

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not say that Goran Jelisic was at the barracks on the 6th of May. I am not aware of that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So when you described, in your OTP statement, seeing somebody called Goran with a bandage, that was someone different from the person you identified in court today, was it?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, that was the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: What I suggest to you is that you simply didn't see Goran Jelisic on the 6th of May because he wasn't, at that stage, injured, didn't have a bandage, so that you may deal with that.

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not see him on the 6th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want to ask you now, please, this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would Your Honour just give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to ask you now, please, about some prisoners who were with you at the barracks. Would this be right? You recognised some of them; Adnan Mustic, Salim Karamehic?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I was with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mirasi? I think I pronounced that badly. Does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Someone you've described as Nermin Suljic, is it possible that that was, in fact, Nermin Suljagic?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: As far as the alleged conversation by the person you've identified as Jelisic about people coming to you later and giving percentages who would be killed and beaten up, I suggest to you that that was never said by Goran Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I claim that he did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you explain, please, why, when you made a statement to the authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you made no mention whatever of that conversation?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: As regards my statement to the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is a case unto itself, because I was almost interrogated when I was giving that statement. Here they read the statement, then they typed it, and what you notice there, you mentioned some names, the names of people that I did not know, and at the time that I gave my statement to the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities, it was immediately in the wake of my exchange and every visit to -- that was the time when planes were shelling, when shells were falling, when there was bombing, when any -- so those were the conditions under which I gave that statement, under which it was worded, and I simply didn't want to go there again because it was so difficult, and I accepted what they showed me that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I understand fully that your circumstances were most difficult. Let me just ask you this: Was that October 1992 when you gave your statement to the authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you sign the statement at the end?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did. It was said that it was merely for internal use, and I did not see any fundamental thing. All they wanted to know was what had been going on, what was happening, so some names, I said that they were typed later, and the statement was put before me. I explained why I didn't want to go there again. I simply wanted to have it over and done with as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I shall be corrected if I'm wrong, but at the conclusion of your statement is this: "At the end, I wish to state I give this statement based on what I personally saw and partly upon what I was told by others in the camp, and I sign it as my own statement. Everything I have included here I am prepared to verify before the court or some international commission which may be interested." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, not really. No, I don't recall it. I'm telling you the state I was in, and in a kind of my self-examination, and I simply was trying to get away from there as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to take any greater length of time, but I want to confirm that that's what he signed, and I wonder whether the original of his Bosnia-Herzegovina statement could be given to him so that he could just identify his signature, please. I don't want to be unfair to him. If we've got the wrong document, then that would be unfair, of course.

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, there is no need. I already said, as regards that statement, I do not see really any fundamental thing except what they added into it subsequently, but I do not think it really affects much things that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. G, do you accept that during the course of that statement, you named a number of people that you recognised at the barracks; Rajko Rajcic, Djordje Ristanic, Mladen Tesic or Teslic, Branislav Stanisavljevic, Ratko Orlic, Zeljko Muminovic, and Zoran Vasilisin?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: At no stage during that statement to the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities did you say, "I had seen Goran at the barracks." Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that I hadn't told them that, really. I telling you that they practically were interrogating me, and I wanted to get rid of them as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want to turn now, please, to your transfer to Luka. At what time of day did your transfer take place?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sometime in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Middle of the afternoon, late afternoon?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: After noon. I cannot be more accurate than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: When you arrived, were there people already there?

utterances.speaker: G (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Were they already inside the hangar, or were they outside, or where were they?
